q: State the formula for density.
Define density.
a: Density is the mass per unit volume of a substance.
It tells us how much mass is packed into each cubic metre.

q: Why does a wooden block float but a steel ball sinks?
a: Less dense objects float; denser objects sink.

q: How do you find the volume of a regular solid?
a: Measure length, width and height with a ruler.

q: How do you find the volume of an irregular solid?
a: Record water volume V₁, lower the object in, record V₂.

q: How do you measure the density of a liquid?
a: Add liquid, measure volume V and new mass (m₂).

q: What equipment measures mass and volume in the density practical?
a: Volume: a ruler (regular) or a measuring cylinder (irregular/liquid)

q: A block has mass 780g and volume 100cm³. Find density in kg/m³.
What fraction of an iceberg floats below the surface?
State the formula for pressure.
What is the unit of pressure?
a: 1 Pa = 1 N/m² (one newton per square metre)

q: How do you INCREASE pressure?
a: Decrease the area (for the same force).
e.g. sharp knife, needle, stiletto heel — small area → high pressure

q: How do you DECREASE pressure?
a: Increase the area (for the same force).
e.g. snowshoes, skis, camel feet, tractor tyres — large area → low pressure

q: In which directions does pressure act in a fluid at rest?
a: EQUALLY in ALL directions at any point.
(upward, downward and sideways — all the same at that depth)

q: Why do camels have wide feet?
a: Large area spreads their weight → lower pressure on the sand → they do not sink in.

q: State the formula for pressure in a liquid.
Why does pressure increase with depth?
a: There is more liquid above pushing down.
The deeper you go, the greater the weight of liquid above → higher pressure.

q: Does pressure in a liquid depend on container shape?
a: NO. It depends only on depth (h) and density (ρ).
Same depth = same pressure in any shaped container.

q: Find the pressure at 15m depth in water (ρ=1000, g=10).
Why are dam walls thicker at the base?
a: Greater force per m² at the base → walls must be stronger/thicker there.

q: What is the total pressure at a depth in a liquid?

q: Define upthrust.
a: The upward force from a fluid on an object.
It equals the weight of the fluid displaced (Archimedes' principle).

q: What is the condition for an object to FLOAT?
a: (net force is zero, so the object stays at the surface)

q: What is the condition for an object to SINK?
a: (net downward force, so the object accelerates down)

q: Why does a huge steel ship float?
a: The hull is hollow (full of air).
The average density of ship + air is LESS than water.

q: How does a submarine sink and rise?
a: Sink: fill ballast tanks with water → weight increases.
Rise: blow water out with compressed air → weight decreases.

q: An object weighs 60N in air, 45N in water. Find the upthrust.
a: Upthrust = weight in air − weight in water

q: Describe the particles in a SOLID.
a: Fixed shape and volume; cannot be compressed.

q: Describe the particles in a LIQUID.
a: Fixed volume, takes shape of container; cannot be compressed.

q: Describe the particles in a GAS.
a: No fixed shape or volume; can be compressed.

q: Why can gases be compressed but not solids or liquids?
a: Gas particles are far apart with large gaps.
Solid/liquid particles are already touching — no space to compress.

q: What happens to gas particles when heated?
a: They move FASTER and spread further apart.
(The particles themselves do NOT change size or expand.)

q: Why does a liquid take the shape of its container?
a: Its particles can move and slide past each other,
but stay close together, so it keeps a fixed volume but no fixed shape.

q: Name the change: solid → liquid.
Name the change: liquid → gas.
What happens to temperature during a change of state?
a: All the energy goes to breaking/forming bonds (latent heat), not changing temperature.

q: At what temperature does ice melt / water boil?
During melting, where does the supplied energy go?
a: It breaks the bonds between particles (increases potential energy).
It does NOT increase kinetic energy, so temperature stays constant.

q: State the formula for specific heat capacity.
Define specific heat capacity.
a: The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C.

q: What is ΔT in ΔQ = mcΔT?
Why is water used as a coolant?
a: Water has a very high SHC (4200 J/kg°C).
It absorbs a lot of energy with only a small temperature rise.

q: In the SHC practical, why insulate the block?
a: To reduce heat loss to the surroundings.
This makes the result more accurate (fair test).

q: Why is the measured SHC usually too high?
a: Some supplied energy heats the surroundings, not just the block.
So the energy per °C appears larger than the true value.

q: State the formula for latent heat.
Define specific latent heat.
a: The energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance WITHOUT a change in temperature.

q: What is latent heat of FUSION?
a: The energy to melt (or freeze) 1 kg at its melting point.

q: What is latent heat of VAPORISATION?
a: The energy to boil (or condense) 1 kg at its boiling point.

q: Find the energy to melt 2kg of ice at 0°C. (L=334,000)
How do you solve a combined mcΔT + mL problem?
a: Do each stage separately: use mL for state changes and mcΔT for temperature changes, then ADD all the energies.

q: What do the SLOPING parts of a heating curve show?
a: Temperature is rising — energy increases kinetic energy of particles.

q: What do the FLAT parts of a heating curve show?
a: A change of state at constant temperature.
Energy breaks bonds — use ΔQ = mL (latent heat).

q: Why is the boiling flat section longer than melting?
a: L_vaporisation (2,260,000) is much larger than L_fusion (334,000).
More energy is needed to fully separate particles into a gas.
